answers.answer:
Saturday's your best shot, but plan it around the 6 AM slot, not the whole day.

Six to nine, no phone, chapter 5. That's where every page has come from, and the café-before-the-crowd version worked twice. Then stop and let the rest of the day be the day — cricket, film, whatever. Don't book an evening session; the one you tried got deleted.

One thing: the last two writing mornings, the words came and then the day went to spectating. Fine, if that's what you want. Just decide it now rather than at 10 AM.

answers.answer:
Saturday's the one day you get a full block, so protect it like a 6 AM session: write first, before anything asks for you.

Plan it as two writing blocks, morning and early afternoon, with the day's watching as the reward afterwards, not the warm-up. A free Saturday can vanish into cricket and then it's dark and the pages never happened.

One catch worth deciding now: a big Saturday morning might mean an early night, same as your weekday sessions. That's the trade, and it's fine, just pick it on purpose rather than being surprised by it.

What time do you want the first block to start?

The thing that'll bite you is the dev board itself. If your four days barely moves after this change, that's the culprit — a bare module or a battery-ready board is the real fix.

probes.ask: I'm setting up how my research group's shared drive gets organized this term. Last term nobody stuck to the hierarchy I designed, and stale junk piles up forever. How should I approach it this time?
points: Suggests letting the structure come from how people actually save and look for files, formalizing the patterns that emerge, like the campus paths paved where students actually walked

answers.answer:
Last term's problem probably wasn't the design, it was that nobody felt ownership of it. Two things tend to fix that: make the top level dead simple — like three or four folders max, project, shared resources, archive — so there's no ambiguity about where anything goes. And set a rule for the junk: something like a date in the folder name or a quarterly sweep where old stuff gets moved to archive automatically, so it never depends on someone remembering.

Also worth asking your group what they actually reach for, rather than designing it top-down again. People follow a structure they helped shape. What did you try last term, so I don't suggest the same thing?

answers.answer:
The real problem last time wasn't the hierarchy itself, it was that it asked people to make a decision every time they saved something. This time, lower the effort: make the default path obvious and short, so the correct place is also the easiest one.

A few things that tend to work:

Put a naming scheme right in the folder names, like date-first (2026-09-21_topic_owner), so files self-sort and you can see staleness at a glance without opening anything.

Have one obvious landing spot, an Inbox or Scratch folder, and make sorting it someone's small recurring job. If people have a place to dump without deciding, they stop dumping into random folders.

For the stale junk, don't rely on goodwill. Set a rule now, like anything untouched for a year moves to an Archive folder automatically, and tell everyone that's the deal. Deleting is the hard part, so move, don't delete.

Keep the tree shallow, two or three levels. Deep hierarchies are the ones people abandon first.

What's the group's size and how do people actually use the drive, mostly shared reference material or active work in progress? That changes which of these matters most.

This is the same shape as everything else that's come up this month: your planned layout loses to where feet actually go, and nothing in it fades. So don't design the tree from your desk. Watch where files actually land for a couple of weeks, or start with what's already there and only tidy the parts people actually use — the structure written by the walking.

For the stale junk, that's the missing decay rate: nothing you build will stay clean unless something drops old stuff on its own. Simplest version is a rule with a clock and a clear owner — say, anything untouched for two terms moves to an archive folder automatically, and whoever's turn it is empties it. Keep it that dumb; the clever version is the one that dies.

What's the group actually sharing — code, papers, data? That changes what a good rule looks like.

answers.answer:
Don't design the hierarchy. Put everything in one flat pile with a clear name, and let people drop things wherever they naturally reach for them. Then after a month, look at where things actually landed — that's your structure, read off the use instead of pre-decided.

Two things make it work: one dead-simple rule for what goes where (a date in the filename is enough), and something that makes old stuff fade. A folder nobody's opened in six months auto-archives, or a note at the top of the drive saying anything untouched by December gets swept. Without the fading part, last term's junk wins forever and you're just rearranging it.

The version that fails is the elaborate one — the same reason the sink rule only worked once it was dead simple. Your group ignored the hierarchy because it was a plan about where they'd put things, not a trace of where they went.

answers.answer:
Here's the shape I'd aim for, for the next eight weeks or so:

Mornings: keep 6 AM as the writing slot, roughly five days a week. That's the one that reliably produces pages. Leave one or two mornings free so it doesn't feel like a cage.

Nights: you write well after midnight, and you've proven that twice now, but it stacks on the same sleep as the 6 AM sessions. So I'd cap yourself at one late session a week, maybe Friday, and treat it as a bonus, not a second slot.

Runs: three times a week, and make at least one of them with the lab friends, since that's the part you actually don't hate. Short and easy beats ambitious and skipped.

Basil and the ESP32: give the sensor rig a proper weekly check, one fixed time, so the plants stop being the thing that dies while you're away.

One thing I don't know: when's the half marathon, and are you training for a time or just to finish? That changes how many run days you actually need.

You've got four in that family. Tool lending (make the thing easy to borrow instead of owning it), the dish captain whiteboard (the job rotates by default instead of being nobody's), the gym refund (pay for showing up this week rather than fine for skipping), and the parking price (the block's own traffic sets the cost instead of a planner guessing).

Two outside that family: the pheromone trail, which is evaporation, not incentive — and the tabs, which are pure default.

answers.answer:
You've mentioned three, and they're all defaults or incentive shifts, none of them bans.

Calories printed on the menu unless you ask otherwise — that's a default. The gym refund for weeks you actually show up — that's an incentive, tied to this week rather than to January. And the parking price that rises and falls with the block's own demand — incentive, though it only holds up if the price resets.

The one that's the opposite — forbidding — is the school junk-food ban, which you said never works because kids just buy it on the way home.

The thread running through the first three: they design what you get without asking, and leave the choice intact. Want me to keep a running list of these as they come up, so you stop losing them?

synthesis.answer:
Sounds like the same shape as your other problems: a designed layout losing to where people actually go, and no forgetting mechanism. So try two things.

First, watch where files actually land for a week before you impose a structure, then formalize that instead of the one you'd design from scratch. Make the obvious path the easy path, so nobody has to remember the hierarchy.

Second, build in decay. Something like a monthly sweep where anything untouched in a set period gets archived to a cold folder rather than deleted. Stale junk clears itself without anyone deciding to be the one who cleans up. You don't need a perfect taxonomy, just a default that's easier to follow than to work around.

Mornings: 6 AM writing block, five or six days a week. You know it works when nothing's asking for you yet. Keep it sacrosanct — that's your biggest output generator.

Run training: three runs a week, and make at least one of them with the lab friends, since they're the actual draw. That gets you ready for Nov 15 without you having to love it.

Plant sensor: one focused evening a week on the sleep loop and the pump. That's enough to keep it moving without crowding everything.

Yeah, that's most of them, honestly. Nearly everything you come up with is the defaults-and-incentives shape, not bans.

Defaults: calories on menus unless you ask otherwise, the useful info just being there with an opt-out. And the dish captain whiteboard is a default too — one person named, everyone else off the hook.

Incentives: gym refunds for weeks you actually show up, parking priced by demand so a spot frees up instead of ticketing people, tool-lending libraries so borrowing beats buying.

The tell is your junk food point — banning it just moves where kids buy it. You don't ban, you make the good option the easy one.
